title: Solve Multiple Percent Equations with List Regression
description: Translate connected percent and percent-change statements with Desmos % of notation, pair them in one list regression, and repair a zero-out fit only when it occurs.

content.html:
Let one regression connect the percent statements

The move: Translate, then pair: write each percent relationship as it sounds and join the equation sides in two lists.

Why it pays: Several comparisons become one calculator entry, without converting each percent into a decimal.

One caution: The amount after of or than is the base of that comparison.

This is an application of list regression. Be comfortable with the basic Percentages lesson and pairing equations in lists; the next screen refreshes that pairing.

Goal: Given several percent relationships, use one list regression to find the requested value and check that its fitted amounts make sense.

Quick refresh: pair the sides

For \(a+b=11\) and \(a-b=3\), put left sides in one list and matching right sides in the other:

\[[a+b,a-b]\sim[11,3]\]

First entries pair together; second entries pair together. The tilde ~ asks Desmos to fit the unknowns. Read the fitted values, change the last 3 to 5, and watch them update. Reset before continuing.

content.hint: Keep each equation’s sides in matching positions, then check the symbol between the lists.
content.prompt: Which single row pairs \(A+B=18\) and \(A-B=6\) correctly?
content.explanation: The first pair says \(A+B=18\); the second says \(A-B=6\). The tilde fits their unknowns together.

content.html:
Keep the percent symbol

“A is 240% of B” translates directly:

\[A=240\%\text{ of }B\]

In Desmos, typing % inserts of automatically; type the base amount after it. Keep a decimal percent such as 0.8% exactly as written, too.

Same English, same order: Do not swap the amount being described with the amount after of.

content.hint: Identify the mass being described, then the mass named after “of.”
content.prompt: A sample’s mass A is 0.8% of mass C. Which equation translates that statement?
content.explanation: A is the described mass; C is the base. Keep 0.8% as written. The other entries reverse the comparison, add an increase, or change the percent.

content.html:
Include the question as one more equation

Sample A has 240% of sample B’s mass and 0.8% of sample C’s mass. B weighs 50 grams. We want p such that C’s mass is p% of B’s mass.

Let A, B, and C represent the masses. Keep the supplied measurement with B=50. Translate the other statements:

  • \(A=240\%\text{ of }B\)
  • \(A=0.8\%\text{ of }C\)
  • \(C=p\%\text{ of }B\)

The last equation makes the requested percent a fitted unknown. Use letters such as A, B, C, and p; lowercase x and y are Desmos graph coordinates.

Three relationships, one tilde

Enter B=50 on one row. On another, enter:

\[[A,A,C]\sim[240\%\text{ of }B,\ 0.8\%\text{ of }C,\ p\%\text{ of }B]\]

A appears twice because two sentences describe A. That is fine inside a list; no separate definitions or rearranging are needed.

REGRESSION PARAMETERS gives \(A=120,C=15000,p=30000\). Read p for the answer. RMSE measures the mismatch between paired entries. Look for zero or a tiny value, then check the original statements.

content.hint: Translate the question using the same “is” and “of” order as a given statement.
content.prompt: The question asks: “C is p% of B.” Which equation belongs in the paired lists?
content.explanation: C is the described amount, p is the unknown percent, and B is its base. Reversing B and C changes the comparison.

content.html:
Build the next pair of lists

Now A is 150% of B, A is 25% of C, and B is 40. Find p if C is p% of B.

The next calculator has the given B=40. Add one list-regression row containing the two comparisons and the requested-percent equation. Use their stated order, with [A,A,C] on the left.

content.title: Translate, then pair

feedback.solution_html: Keep \(B=40\). Enter \([A,A,C]\sim[150\%\text{ of }B,25\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\). Desmos fits \(A=60,C=240,p=600\).
feedback.retry_message_html: Keep B=40. Check the order of the three percent entries, including which amount follows each “of.”
feedback.success_message_html: The three percent statements are paired correctly. Read p and check the fit.

content.instructions_html: B is 40. A is 150% of B and 25% of C. C is p% of B. Keep B=40 and add one regression row using [A,A,C] on the left and matching percent expressions on the right. Use the percent symbol in each entry.

content.hint: Read the fitted parameter for the requested percent, rather than one of the fitted amounts.
content.prompt: In the problem you just entered, A is 150% of B, A is 25% of C, and B is 40. If C is p% of B, what is p?
content.solution:
Enter \(B=40\), then \([A,A,C]\sim[150\%\text{ of }B,25\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\).
Read \(p=600\) under REGRESSION PARAMETERS. Report 600, not C or C/B.
content.explanation: The fitted p is 600. C is six times B, which is 600% of B.

content.html:
What if no mass is given?

Return to A being 240% of B and 0.8% of C, with C equal to p% of B. This time, no mass is specified.

In a fresh calculator, enter the three-pair list regression directly. Let Desmos try first. If it returns positive masses, zero or tiny RMSE, and values that satisfy the statements, read p. There is no extra value to assign.

The individual masses can vary, but their relative sizes and the requested percent stay fixed. A valid positive fit gives \(p=30000\).

If the amounts zero out

Inspect the result before changing the setup. If Desmos returns \(A=B=C=0\), the equations reduce to zero equals zero for any p. Even zero RMSE cannot determine the requested percent from that fit.

Only if this happens, add B=1 and let the regression refit A, C, and p. Here B is a free reference amount, so one positive value sets the scale without changing the percent comparison.

The repaired fit gives \(A=2.4,C=300,p=30000\). If the result remains unreliable, recheck the entries and use another method.

Repair the result you see: Try the regression, inspect the amounts, then fix one free base if they zero out.

content.hint: The result already satisfies the equations and the positive-mass context.
content.prompt: With no given mass, Desmos returns positive masses that satisfy every percent statement and zero RMSE. What should you do?
choices: Replace every fitted mass with 1 and run again.
Define B=1 before using any fitted percent.
Report RMSE as the requested percent value.
Read the requested percent from the fitted p.
content.explanation: A valid positive fit already answers the question. Setting a free base is a response to a zero-out result, not a required first step.

content.hint: A free reference amount sets the scale. The other amounts and the requested percent still need to satisfy the relationships.
content.prompt: No actual mass is given. Your percent equations return A=B=C=0, although the samples have positive masses. What is the appropriate repair?
choices: Accept p because the RMSE is zero.
Set one free mass, such as B, to 1 and refit.
Set every mass to 1 and keep the same p.
Replace the requested percent p with 1 and refit.
content.explanation: Fix one free positive base and let the other values refit. Defining every mass would conflict with the comparisons; fixing p would choose the answer.

content.html:
A supplied value is not a free base

If the question gives \(B=75\) grams, keep B=75. Replacing it with 1 changes the stated measurement.

A reference value is safe in the previous example because only relative sizes are fixed and the question asks for a percent. If a question asks for an actual mass but gives only ratios, choosing a base cannot uncover a unique mass.

content.hint: Use the measurement supplied by the question.
content.prompt: A percent-equations problem gives B=75 grams. Which definition should the calculator use?
content.explanation: Keep B=75. A convenient reference value cannot replace an actual stated quantity.

content.html:
Greater than and less than keep the old amount

Use the percent-change template from the Percentages lesson:

\[\text{New}=\text{Old}\pm p\%\text{ of Old}\]

“A is 20% greater than B” becomes \(A=B+20\%\text{ of }B\). “A is 25% less than C” becomes \(A=C-25\%\text{ of }C\).

The amount after than is the base. Pair these sides exactly as written; do not subtract 20 and 25 to compare B with C.

content.hint: Start with the amount named after “than,” then subtract a percent of that same amount.
content.prompt: A is 25% less than C. Which equation preserves the base and the remaining amount?
content.explanation: Start with C and subtract 25% of C. The other choices keep just the removed part, use A as the base, or make an increase.

content.html:
The lists work the same way

If A is 20% greater than B and 25% less than C, and C is p% of B, enter:

\[[A,A,C]\sim[B+20\%\text{ of }B,\ C-25\%\text{ of }C,\ p\%\text{ of }B]\]

Try it directly. Inspect the fitted amounts and RMSE. If the amounts zero out, set the free reference amount B=1 and rerun. A valid positive fit gives \(p=160\).

The question asks what percent C is of B, not the percent increase from B to C.

content.prompt: A is 50% greater than B and 20% less than C. All three quantities are positive. If C is p% of B, what is the value of p?
content.explanation: Enter \([A,A,C]\sim[B+50\%\text{ of }B,C-20\%\text{ of }C,p\%\text{ of }B]\). Inspect the fit; if the amounts zero out, define the free base \(B=1\) and rerun. A valid positive fit gives \(p=187.5\).

content.prompt: Recall “translate, then pair.” Which routine carries several percent statements through to an answer?
choices: Translate with % of; pair matching sides with ~; check the amounts; report RMSE as the requested percent.
Translate with % of; pair sides in separate orders with ~; check the fit and read the requested value.
Translate with % of; pair matching sides with ~; check the fit and read the requested value; repair a zero-out result if needed.
Translate with % of; fix each unknown amount at 1; pair matching sides with ~; check the fit and read the requested value.
content.explanation: Translate each comparison, including the requested one. Matching list positions preserve the statements. Inspect the fit before making any manual assignment, and preserve given quantities.

content.html:
Put it together

Start with a fresh scratch calculator for the final problem. Translate the statements, build the paired lists, and inspect the fit before deciding whether it needs a repair.

content.prompt: The mass of sample R is 360% of the mass of sample S and 0.9% of the mass of sample T. The samples have positive masses. If the mass of sample T is \(q\%\) of the mass of sample S, what is the value of \(q\)?
content.explanation: Enter \([R,R,T]\sim[360\%\text{ of }S,0.9\%\text{ of }T,q\%\text{ of }S]\). Read q from a valid positive fit. If the masses zero out, define the free base \(S=1\) and refit; then \(R=3.6,T=400,q=40000\). Report the percent 40000.

content.html:
Translate, then pair

When percent statements connect several quantities, let one list regression connect them for you.
